blocks.prompt: The Berry That Is Not a Berry
blocks.text: A strawberry starts out as a white flower. A bee lands on the flower and moves the pollen around. Then the petals fall off. The middle of the flower begins to swell. It gets bigger and bigger. It turns from green to white to red. Most people call the little dots on the outside seeds. One strawberry can have about two hundred of them. The plant does something else that is clever. It sends out a long green arm called a runner. The runner reaches across the dirt and puts down roots. Now there is a brand new plant.

blocks.prompt: The Dots Are the Real Fruit
blocks.text: Bite into a strawberry and you are eating something strange. The soft red part is not the fruit at all. It is the swollen middle of the flower, and it grew fat to hold something up: the little dots. Each dot is called an achene. Say it like this: ay-KEEN. Each achene is a tiny dry fruit, and each one holds one seed. So a strawberry is not one fruit. It is about two hundred tiny fruits riding on a red cushion. The cushion has a job. It is sweet and bright so that birds and animals will eat it and carry the seeds away. There is one more surprise. Every one of those dots has to be pollinated, and bees do most of that work as they carry pollen from flower to flower. If a dot gets missed, the red part underneath it never swells. That is why some strawberries come out lumpy and crooked. The shape of a strawberry is a map of where the bees went.

notes: Not a berry, botanically

blocks.prompt: A Fruit That Is Not a Berry
blocks.text: Botanists have a rule for what counts as a berry, and the strawberry breaks it. A true berry grows from a single ovary in the flower and holds its seeds inside. By that rule, a grape is a berry. A tomato is a berry. A banana is a berry. A strawberry is not. What we eat is the receptacle: the small pad at the base of the flower that once held the petals. After pollination, that pad balloons outward, floods with sugar and with red pigments called anthocyanins, and becomes the thing in your hand. The actual fruits are the dots stuck to its surface. Each dot, called an achene, is a dry one-seeded fruit of its own. Because the strawberry is built from many fruits arranged on a fleshy base, botanists call it an aggregate accessory fruit. Accessory means the tasty part came from something other than the ovary. The strawberry belongs to the rose family, which makes it a cousin of apples, cherries, almonds, and roses themselves. That family resemblance shows in the flower: five white petals, a crowd of yellow stamens, and a scent you can pick up from a step away. One more thing separates a strawberry from a banana. A banana keeps ripening after you pick it. A strawberry does not. It softens, it dulls, it eventually spoils, but it will never get sweeter than the moment it left the plant. Whatever sweetness it has, it earned in the field.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Was Invented by Accident
blocks.text: For most of human history, a strawberry was a small thing. The wild woodland strawberry of Europe, Fragaria vesca, produces fruit about the size of a fingernail. It is intensely fragrant and it is gone in two bites. People gathered it from forest edges for thousands of years and never expected more. The strawberry you know is barely three hundred years old, and nobody set out to make it. Early in the 1700s, a French military engineer named Amedee-Francois Frezier sailed to Chile. His official job was mapping harbors and fortifications for the king. Along the coast he found farmers growing a strawberry with fruit the size of a walnut. He dug up five plants and kept them alive for six months at sea by sharing his own drinking water with them. They reached France in 1714. They flowered. They did not fruit. Frezier had, without knowing it, collected only female plants. The Chilean strawberry keeps its males and females on separate plants, and he had left every male behind in South America. The plants were parceled out to gardens in Brittany. Someone set them near a different import: Fragaria virginiana, a smaller strawberry brought from eastern North America and prized for its deep flavor. Bees did the rest. The cross produced a plant with the size of one parent and the flavor of the other, and its fruit smelled faintly of pineapple. Gardeners named it the pineapple strawberry, Fragaria ananassa. The person who worked out what had happened was a teenager. Antoine Nicolas Duchesne, nineteen years old, studied the strawberry beds at Versailles, tracked which plants had crossed with which, and published his findings in 1766. He showed that a brand new kind of fruit had appeared in a garden, made by two species from two continents that had never met at home. Almost every strawberry sold today descends from that accident.

6.title: The Berry That Is Not a Berry
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Berry That Is Not a Berry

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fragaria x ananassa, rose family
Aggregate accessory fruit, not a berry
About 200 achenes per fruit
Hormones from each achene tell the flesh to swell
Runners produce clones, not seeds
Hybrid origin: chiloensis crossed with virginiana

blocks.prompt: The Strawberry Is Not What You Think It Is
blocks.text: Almost everything you assume about a strawberry is wrong, starting with the word berry. Botany defines a berry as a fruit that develops from a single ovary and carries its seeds inside its own flesh. Grapes qualify. Tomatoes qualify. Bananas qualify. The strawberry fails on both counts. The red flesh did not grow from an ovary at all. It grew from the receptacle, the small pad at the center of the flower where the petals attach. After pollination that pad swells, loads itself with sugars and with red pigments called anthocyanins, and presents itself to the world as fruit. It is, in the strictest sense, a costume. The real fruits are the dots. Each one is an achene, a dry, hard, single-seeded fruit no bigger than a comma, and an average strawberry carries around two hundred of them. So the object in your hand is not a fruit. It is roughly two hundred fruits standing on a sweet red platform. Botanists file it under aggregate accessory fruit, where aggregate means many and accessory means the delicious part came from somewhere it had no business coming from. The arrangement has consequences. Each achene must be pollinated separately, and each pollinated achene releases hormones that tell the tissue directly beneath it to swell. Fertilize every dot and the receptacle expands evenly into the shape people expect. Miss a patch, and the flesh under that patch stays flat. A lumpy, pinched, lopsided strawberry is not a defective strawberry. It is an honest record of which flowers the bees did not finish. The plant hedges its bets in a second way. Alongside seeds, a strawberry sends out runners, long horizontal stems that crawl across the soil, stop, and put down roots. The new plant is a clone, genetically identical to its parent, and it can do the same thing again. One plant becomes a colony. This is why a strawberry field can be, in effect, a single individual copied across acres, and why a disease that defeats one plant defeats all of them. The last surprise is that the strawberry on your plate is an invention, and a recent one. Europe's native woodland strawberry is the size of a fingernail. The large fruit came from Chile, carried to France in 1714 by an engineer named Amedee-Francois Frezier, who kept five plants alive at sea by sharing his water ration. His plants were all female and produced nothing. Only when they were set in French gardens beside a strawberry imported from eastern North America, and bees crossed the two, did the modern strawberry exist at all. A teenage botanist named Antoine Nicolas Duchesne worked out what had happened and published it in 1766, at nineteen. Two species from two continents that had never shared a habitat produced, by accident, in a garden, the fruit now grown on every inhabited continent. Consider what the strawberry actually is, then. Not a berry. Not one fruit. Not ancient. Not, in any strict sense, wild. It is a swollen flower base wearing two hundred fruits, spread by cloning, invented three centuries ago by two plants that had never met, and a bee.
